summary: This chapter covers what an inspector checks while walking around the outside of the house: the ground around it, paths and driveways, decks and steps, the wall coverings, and the windows and doors. Most of these items have one job in common, which is keeping water away from the house and keeping people from getting hurt.

Water is the main enemy. The ground next to the foundation should slope away so rain runs off instead of soaking down along the walls. Under common model codes the ground typically drops at least 6 inches within the first 10 feet. Siding and wood trim should stay well above the soil, and flashing must lap over the material below it so water is led outward, not behind the wall.

Decks fail in a few predictable places. The ledger board that ties the deck to the house must be bolted or lag-screwed and flashed, never held up by nails alone. Guards are typically required once the deck surface is more than 30 inches above the ground, and stairs need even steps and a usable handrail.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, the ground next to the foundation typically falls at least 6 inches within the first 10 feet. Flat or reverse slope sends rain toward the walls and can lead to wet basements and settling.
concepts.tip: Think "6 in 10": six inches of drop in ten feet.

concepts.definition: Wood and wood-based siding should not sit on or near the soil. Under common model codes, wood closer than about 6 inches to exposed ground must be rot-resistant or treated. Soil against siding also gives insects a hidden path.
concepts.tip: If you can't see a gap between soil and siding, write it up.

concepts.definition: Thin metal or membrane pieces that guide water out and away at joints, such as over windows and doors and where a deck or roof meets a wall. Upper pieces must lap over lower pieces, like shingles.
concepts.tip: Water runs downhill: every layer should lap over the one below it.

concepts.definition: The board that fastens a deck to the house. Under common model codes it is attached with bolts or lag screws, not nails alone, and flashed so water does not rot the house framing behind it.
concepts.tip: A nailed-only ledger is a safety item. Many deck collapses start here.

concepts.definition: Guards are typically required where a walking surface is more than 30 inches above the ground below. Under common model codes they are at least 36 inches high, with openings small enough that a 4-inch ball cannot pass through (guards along the open side of stairs may allow up to 4 3/8 inches).
concepts.tip: Remember 30 / 36 / 4: when needed, how tall, how wide the gaps.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, home stair risers are typically no more than 7 3/4 inches high and treads at least 10 inches deep. Steps in one flight should be nearly the same size so people do not trip.
concepts.tip: Uneven steps cause falls even when each step is within the limit.

points: Negative grading or downspouts dumping at the foundation are frequent findings.
Look for missing flashing above windows, doors, and at the deck ledger.
Deck guards and stairs are life-safety items; report them clearly.
Trees and shrubs touching the house hold moisture and give pests a bridge.

summary: This chapter is about the roof covering, the flashing that seals its edges and openings, and the gutters that carry water away. The inspector's job is to describe the covering, look for wear and damage, and point out places where water is likely to get in.

Asphalt shingles are the most common covering. As they age they lose their granules, curl or cup at the edges, crack, and blister. Under common model codes they are typically not used on slopes below 2 in 12, and slopes from 2 in 12 up to 4 in 12 need extra underlayment. Missing or lifted shingles after wind should always be noted.

Most leaks start at flashing, not in the middle of the roof. Look closely where the roof meets a wall, at chimneys, in valleys, and around vent pipes. Gutters should be clean and sloped to downspouts, and downspouts should drop water well away from the foundation.

concepts.definition: Common signs of aging asphalt shingles are granule loss, curling or cupping edges, cracks, and blisters. Granules piled in gutters or at downspout outlets are a clue that the surface is wearing away.
concepts.tip: Bare dark spots and curled tabs mean the roof is near the end of its life.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, asphalt shingles are typically installed only on slopes of 2 in 12 or more. Between 2 in 12 and 4 in 12, a double layer of underlayment is required.
concepts.tip: Below 2 in 12, shingles are the wrong material for the job.

concepts.definition: Small L-shaped metal pieces woven in with each course of shingles where a sloped roof meets a sidewall. Each piece laps over the one below, and the wall covering laps over the flashing.
concepts.tip: One piece per shingle course. Shingle makers call for step flashing, so a single long strip is worth noting.

concepts.definition: A chimney needs base flashing plus counterflashing set into the masonry. Under common model codes, a cricket (small peaked diverter) is typically required on the uphill side when the chimney is wider than 30 inches.
concepts.tip: Wide chimney, uphill side: look for the cricket.

concepts.definition: Metal edging at the eaves and rakes that lets water drip clear of the fascia. Under common model codes it is typically required for asphalt shingle roofs.
concepts.tip: Look along the roof edge for a metal lip under the first course.

concepts.definition: Gutters collect roof water and should slope toward downspouts. Downspouts should discharge onto splash blocks or extensions that carry water away from the foundation.
concepts.tip: A downspout dumping at the wall undoes good grading.

points: Leaks most often start at flashing: walls, chimneys, valleys, and pipe boots.
Note the roof covering type and any areas you could not see or walk.
Exposed nail heads and lifted tabs invite water and wind damage.
Granules in the gutters point to worn shingles.

summary: This chapter covers the parts that hold the house up: footings, foundation walls, posts, beams, joists, and the crawlspace or basement around them. The inspector looks for signs that the structure has moved or is being damaged by water, and explains how serious those signs appear to be.

Cracks tell a story by their shape. Thin vertical cracks in poured concrete are often from normal shrinkage. Stair-step cracks in block or brick suggest settling, and horizontal cracks in a block wall can mean soil pressure is pushing the wall inward. Wide cracks, cracks that are offset, or walls that lean deserve a referral to a structural engineer.

Framing members can be weakened by careless cuts. Under common model codes, notches and holes in joists are limited in size and location. Moisture is the other big threat: look for efflorescence on masonry, water stains, wood rot, and poor crawlspace ventilation.

concepts.definition: The wide base under a foundation wall or post that spreads the house's weight over the soil. In cold areas the bottom of the footing must sit below the local frost depth so freezing soil does not lift it.
concepts.tip: No footing, or a post sitting on bare dirt, is a structural concern.

concepts.definition: Thin vertical cracks in poured concrete are often shrinkage. Stair-step cracks in masonry suggest settlement. Horizontal cracks in block walls often mean soil is pushing the wall in. Wide, offset, or growing cracks need an engineer.
concepts.tip: Horizontal crack plus inward bow in a block wall = refer to an engineer.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, notches in sawn lumber joists are typically limited to one-sixth of the depth and are not allowed in the middle third of the span. Bored holes are limited to one-third of the depth and kept at least 2 inches from the top and bottom edges.
concepts.tip: Notches at the ends are allowed if small; notches mid-span are not.

concepts.definition: White, powdery salt deposits left on concrete or masonry when water moves through the wall and evaporates. It is not harmful by itself but shows that moisture is getting through.
concepts.tip: White powder on basement walls means water has been there.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, a vented crawlspace typically needs at least 1 square foot of vent opening for each 150 square feet of floor area. With a ground vapor retarder this can drop to 1 per 1,500. Sealed crawlspaces are another allowed design.
concepts.tip: Remember 1 in 150, or 1 in 1,500 with a vapor retarder.

points: Describe crack type, size, and location rather than guessing the cause.
Refer wide, offset, or horizontal cracks to a structural engineer.
Check posts for solid bearing and secure connections to beams.
Water stains, rot, and standing water in crawlspaces are common findings.

compare.title: Reading foundation cracks
rows: Describe; refer if wide or offset

summary: This chapter follows electricity from the utility wires to the outlets. It covers the service entrance, the main panel, branch circuits, grounding and bonding, and the special protective devices called GFCIs and AFCIs. Electrical findings are often safety items, so clear reporting matters.

Overhead service wires need enough clearance so people cannot touch them. Under the National Electrical Code they are typically at least 10 feet above finished grade and walkways. At the panel, the inspector checks for proper working space, matching wire and breaker sizes, double-tapped breakers, scorching, and missing covers or knockouts.

Wire size must match the breaker. In common practice, 14-gauge copper is protected at 15 amps, 12-gauge at 20 amps, and 10-gauge at 30 amps. GFCIs protect people from shock in wet areas, while AFCIs reduce fire risk from arcing in living areas. Test them where safe and note any that do not trip.

concepts.definition: Under the National Electrical Code, overhead service wires are typically at least 10 feet above finished grade, sidewalks, and areas reached only by people on foot. Higher clearances apply over driveways and streets.
concepts.tip: 10 feet is the minimum over walking areas.

concepts.definition: Under the National Electrical Code, the space in front of a panel is typically at least 30 inches wide, 36 inches deep, and 6 1/2 feet high, kept clear of storage.
concepts.tip: Think 30 wide, 36 deep: room to stand and work safely.

concepts.definition: For copper branch wiring the common limits are: 14 AWG on 15 amps, 12 AWG on 20 amps, and 10 AWG on 30 amps. A breaker too large for its wire lets the wire overheat before the breaker trips.
concepts.tip: Smaller gauge number = thicker wire = more amps allowed.

concepts.definition: Two wires under one breaker screw that is made for only one. It can loosen and overheat. Some breakers are listed for two wires; most are not.
concepts.tip: Two wires, one screw: report it unless the breaker is labeled for it.

concepts.definition: A ground-fault circuit interrupter cuts power when current leaks to ground, protecting people from shock. Under the National Electrical Code it is typically required in bathrooms, garages, outdoors, crawlspaces, basements, kitchens, laundry areas, and near sinks.
concepts.tip: GFCI = people protection in wet or damp places.

concepts.definition: An arc-fault circuit interrupter detects dangerous sparking in wiring and shuts the circuit off to help prevent fires. Under the National Electrical Code it is typically required for most living-area circuits such as bedrooms, living rooms, and kitchens.
concepts.tip: AFCI = fire protection in living spaces.

concepts.definition: Grounding connects the system to the earth; bonding ties metal parts together so a fault trips the breaker. Neutral and ground wires are joined only at the main service; in subpanels they are kept on separate bars.
concepts.tip: Neutrals and grounds together in a subpanel is a defect.

points: Check that each breaker matches the wire it protects.
Report double taps, scorching, open knockouts, and missing panel screws.
Test GFCIs where safe; note required locations without protection.
Do not confuse GFCI (shock) with AFCI (fire).
Panels with known problem histories should be referred to an electrician.

compare.title: GFCI vs. AFCI
rows: Wet and damp areas: baths, kitchens, basements, garages, outdoors
Living areas: bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens

summary: This chapter covers the equipment that heats and cools the house: furnaces, boilers, heat pumps, and central air conditioners, along with their venting and ducts. The inspector operates the system with normal controls, looks at what is visible, and reports conditions that affect safety or comfort.

Fuel-burning equipment needs enough air to burn cleanly and a vent that carries exhaust gases outside. Under common model codes, a natural-draft vent connector typically rises at least 1/4 inch per foot toward the chimney, and single-wall metal connectors are kept about 6 inches from combustibles. Backdrafting, rust, scorching near the burner, or a flame that jumps when the blower starts can point to a cracked heat exchanger and carbon monoxide risk.

Air conditioners and heat pumps move heat using refrigerant. In cooling mode, the larger, insulated line is the cool suction line and the smaller line is the warm liquid line. Cooling makes water, so condensate must drain properly, and units above finished space typically need a secondary drain or a pan with a shutoff switch.

concepts.definition: Fuel-burning appliances need a steady supply of air to burn fuel completely. A furnace closed into a small room without enough air can produce carbon monoxide and spill exhaust into the house.
concepts.tip: Small closet, no air openings = possible combustion air problem.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, a natural-draft vent connector typically slopes upward at least 1/4 inch per foot toward the chimney or vent. Single-wall metal connectors are typically kept at least 6 inches from combustible material.
concepts.tip: Exhaust must always travel uphill to the chimney.

source.org: International Residential Code, Fuel Gas chapter (ICC)

concepts.definition: The metal chamber inside a furnace that keeps burning gases separate from house air. A crack can let exhaust mix with the air you breathe. Clues include rust, soot, a flame that wavers when the blower starts, and high carbon monoxide.
concepts.tip: Flame dancing when the blower turns on = refer to an HVAC technician.

concepts.definition: Split air conditioners and heat pumps have two copper lines. In cooling mode, the larger suction line carries cool vapor and should be insulated; the smaller liquid line carries warm liquid. Missing or damaged insulation is a common finding.
concepts.tip: Big line cool and wrapped; small line warm and bare.

concepts.definition: Cooling equipment produces water that must drain to an approved place. Under common model codes, units where overflow could damage finished areas typically need a secondary drain, a pan, or a float switch that shuts the unit off.
concepts.tip: Attic air handler? Look for the pan and the backup drain.

concepts.definition: The difference between return air and supply air while cooling. A split of roughly 14 to 22 degrees F is a common rule of thumb for normal operation; readings far outside it suggest a service call.
concepts.tip: Too small a split means it is not cooling well.

points: Carbon monoxide and venting issues are safety items; report them first.
Check vent connectors for slope, clearance, rust, and loose joints.
Look for condensate leaks, missing pans, and clogged drains.
Operate equipment with normal controls only; do not force it in extreme weather.
Recommend service by a licensed HVAC technician for suspected defects.

summary: This chapter covers the water that comes into the house and the water that leaves it. It includes supply piping, the drain-waste-vent system, water heaters, and fixtures. The inspector runs water, checks for leaks and poor drainage, and looks for missing safety parts.

Every fixture drain has a trap, a bend that stays filled with water so sewer gas cannot come up into the room. Under common model codes the water seal is typically 2 to 4 inches deep. The trap arm runs from the trap to the vent and slopes slightly downhill, typically 1/4 inch per foot for small pipes. The vent lets air into the system so draining water does not siphon the trap dry. S-traps are not allowed because they tend to siphon.

The water heater must have a temperature and pressure relief valve. Its discharge pipe should be full size, run downhill, have no valve or threads at the end, and typically end no more than 6 inches above the floor or at an approved location. Supply pipe material matters too: polybutylene and old galvanized steel are known for failures.

concepts.definition: A trap is a curved section under a fixture that holds water. That water, called the trap seal, blocks sewer gas. Under common model codes the seal is typically at least 2 inches and no more than 4 inches deep.
concepts.tip: Seal depth: 2 to 4 inches.

concepts.definition: The highest point inside the trap outlet, where water spills over into the trap arm. The standing water in the trap stays level with the weir, so the seal depth is measured from the weir down to the top of the dip.
concepts.tip: Water can only stand as high as the weir.

concepts.definition: The pipe from the trap outlet to the vent connection. Under common model codes it typically slopes 1/4 inch per foot for pipes 2 1/2 inches and smaller, and its length is limited by pipe size.
concepts.tip: Too long or too steep, and the trap can siphon dry.

concepts.definition: A pipe that lets air into the drain system and lets sewer gas escape above the roof. It keeps pressure even so water rushing down the drain does not suck the trap empty.
concepts.tip: Gurgling drains and slow draining often point to venting problems.

concepts.definition: A trap whose outlet turns straight down instead of running level to a vent. It tends to siphon itself dry. Under common model codes S-traps are not allowed.
concepts.tip: Outlet turns down = S-trap = report it.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, the water heater relief valve pipe is full size, drains by gravity, has no valve or threaded end, and typically ends no more than 6 inches above the floor or at another approved place.
concepts.tip: Full size, downhill, no valve, no threads, 6 inches from the floor.

concepts.definition: Common supply pipes are copper, PEX, and CPVC. Gray polybutylene and old galvanized steel are known for leaks and clogging and are often flagged for further review.
concepts.tip: Gray plastic supply pipe? Note possible polybutylene.

points: The trap seal water stands level with the trap weir.
The trap arm slopes slightly downward toward the vent and stack.
S-traps and missing traps let sewer gas into the house.
A capped, valved, or upward-running TPR discharge pipe is a safety item.
Run water at fixtures to check flow, drainage, and leaks below.

figures.alt: A sink tailpiece drops into a U-shaped P-trap holding water. The water surface lines up with the trap weir, the high point inside the trap outlet. The trap arm runs from the trap to a vertical stack, sloping slightly down; the stack goes up as the vent and down as the drain.
figures.caption: Parts of a P-trap: the seal water stands level with the weir.

summary: This chapter covers the inside of the house and the attic above it. It includes walls, floors, ceilings, stairs, windows and doors, insulation and ventilation, fireplaces, and built-in appliances. Many items here are about comfort, but some, like stairs, alarms, and fireplaces, are about safety.

In the attic, look at how much insulation there is, whether it is spread evenly, and whether air can move through. Under common model codes, attic vent area is typically 1 square foot for every 150 square feet of attic floor, or 1 per 300 when vents are balanced high and low. Bath fans and dryer vents must go outside, not into the attic.

Fireplaces need a solid hearth extension in front and to the sides, and the chimney must be tall enough to draw well. Smoke alarms belong in each bedroom, outside sleeping areas, and on every level, and carbon monoxide alarms are typically needed when the home has fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, a vented attic typically needs 1 square foot of net vent area per 150 square feet of attic floor. This can drop to 1 per 300 when vents are split between high and low locations.
concepts.tip: 1 in 150, or 1 in 300 with balanced high and low vents.

concepts.definition: Bathroom fans, ducted kitchen exhaust, and clothes dryers must vent to the outside. Ending them in the attic or crawlspace puts moisture and lint where they cause mold and fire risk.
concepts.tip: Follow the duct: it must leave the building.

concepts.definition: The fireproof floor in front of a fireplace. Under common model codes, for an opening under 6 square feet it typically extends at least 16 inches in front and 8 inches past each side.
concepts.tip: 16 in front, 8 to the sides for a smaller fireplace.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, a chimney typically extends at least 3 feet above where it leaves the roof and at least 2 feet higher than any part of the building within 10 feet.
concepts.tip: 3 feet up, 2 feet higher than anything within 10 feet.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, smoke alarms go in each sleeping room, outside each sleeping area, and on each story. Carbon monoxide alarms are typically required outside sleeping areas when there are fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage.
concepts.tip: Every bedroom, every hallway outside bedrooms, every level.

concepts.definition: Under common model codes, stair handrails are typically 34 to 38 inches high, measured from the nosing of the treads.
concepts.tip: Handrails 34 to 38 inches; guards at floor edges at least 36 inches.

points: Bath and dryer vents ending in the attic are frequent findings.
Note missing, compressed, or uneven attic insulation.
Check for missing smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.
Look inside the firebox and flue where accessible; refer cracks to a chimney professional.
Water stains on ceilings should be checked with a moisture meter when possible.

summary: This chapter is about turning what you saw into a report the client can understand and act on. A good finding does three things: it describes what was observed, explains why it matters, and recommends a next step. The report is the product the client pays for, so clarity matters as much as accuracy.

Not every defect is equal. Safety issues and major defects that could be costly come first, while routine maintenance items come after. Inspectors are generalists, so when a problem needs deeper evaluation, the right recommendation is to have a qualified specialist look at it rather than guessing the repair.

Use plain words and specific locations. Say what you saw, not what you assume, and avoid vague phrases that leave the client unsure. State any areas you could not inspect and why, such as a locked door, stored items, or unsafe access.

concepts.definition: A clear finding states what was seen and where, explains what could happen if it is left alone, and tells the client what to do next and who should do it.
concepts.tip: What? So what? Now what?

concepts.definition: A problem with a system or component that may significantly affect the home's value or pose an unreasonable risk to people. It is not simply something old or cosmetic.
concepts.tip: Old is not the same as defective; ask if it really harms value or safety.

concepts.definition: Safety items can injure people, such as missing guards, exposed wiring, or a capped relief valve. Maintenance items are routine upkeep, such as caulking or cleaning gutters. Reports should make the difference obvious.
concepts.tip: Put safety first so the client cannot miss it.

concepts.definition: When a condition is outside a generalist's scope or needs testing, the inspector recommends evaluation by a qualified professional, such as a licensed electrician or structural engineer.
concepts.tip: Refer the problem; do not diagnose beyond what you saw.

concepts.definition: The report should name parts of the home that were not inspected or only partly inspected and give the reason, such as no access, snow cover, or utilities turned off.
concepts.tip: If you didn't see it, say so and say why.

points: Every finding should state location, condition, why it matters, and the next step.
Separate safety items and major defects from maintenance.
Recommend a qualified specialist instead of guessing repair methods.
Avoid vague words like "appears fine" without saying what was checked.
List areas not inspected and the reasons.

compare.title: Safety item vs. maintenance item
rows: Correct promptly by a qualified pro

summary: This chapter covers how a home inspector should conduct business: what the inspection includes and excludes, how to avoid conflicts of interest, and how to set expectations with a written agreement. These topics protect both the client and the inspector.

A home inspection is a visual, non-invasive look at readily accessible systems and components on the day of the inspection. Under typical standards of practice, the inspector does not move furniture, take things apart, or enter areas that are unsafe. It is also not a code compliance inspection and does not guarantee future performance.

Inspectors work for their clients, not for agents or sellers. They should not take fees from contractors for referrals, should disclose any relationships that could affect their judgment, and should not offer to repair things they found during the inspection. A written pre-inspection agreement explains the scope, limits, and fee before the work begins, and the report is shared only with the client's permission.

concepts.definition: The inspection covers what can be seen and reached safely without moving belongings, removing finishes, or taking equipment apart. Hidden conditions behind walls or under carpet are outside the scope.
concepts.tip: If it needs tools to open or move, it is usually out of scope.

concepts.definition: A home inspection reports on condition and safety, not on whether the home meets the building code in force when it was built. Inspectors may use code ideas as guidance but do not certify code compliance.
concepts.tip: Write "safety concern," not "code violation."

concepts.definition: Any relationship that could tempt an inspector to shade the report, such as paying agents for referrals or taking kickbacks from repair contractors. Such relationships should be avoided or clearly disclosed.
concepts.tip: Loyalty goes to the client who hired you.

concepts.definition: Inspectors should not offer to repair conditions they found in their own inspection. Doing so creates a motive to find or exaggerate problems.
concepts.tip: Find it, report it, but don't sell the fix.

concepts.definition: A written contract signed before the inspection that describes what will and will not be inspected, the standards followed, limitations, and the fee.
concepts.tip: Get it signed before you start.

concepts.definition: The report belongs to the client. The inspector should not share it with others, such as the seller or another buyer, without the client's permission unless the law requires it.
concepts.tip: Ask the client before sending the report to anyone else.

points: Home inspections are visual and limited to readily accessible areas.
Inspectors are not required to move belongings or enter unsafe spaces.
Avoid referral fees and disclose any relationship that could bias you.
Do not offer repairs on homes you inspected.
Use a written agreement and keep the report confidential.

compare.title: Home inspection vs. code inspection
rows: An inspector hired by the client (often a buyer)
